column2: [Bhishma said:] Hearing the words of the seeker of dharma, the guest, a wise one, spoke gentle words in a sweet voice:

I too am bewildered here; this is my wish too; and I come to no settled conclusion, for heaven has many doors.
mahabharata:12:342.11	Some rely on the dharma of kings, some on the fruit of the self, some on service of the teacher, some on the word of restraint.
mahabharata:12:342.12	Some have gone to heaven serving mother and father; others by non-violence, others by truth.
mahabharata:12:342.13	Some, facing the enemy in battle, were slain and went to heaven; some became perfected by gleaning vows, resorting to the path of heaven.
mahabharata:12:342.14	Some, devoted to study, intent on the Vedic vows, good, wise, content in self and masters of their senses, went to heaven.
mahabharata:12:342.15	Others joined with honesty, slain by dishonest men, the honest, pure of soul, are established in the vault of heaven.
mahabharata:12:342.16	Thus, with the many kinds of doors of dharma open in the world, my mind too is troubled, like a line of cloud by the wind.

Having made his dwelling there, the righteous-souled one, the great Padmanabha, called the Eye-Hearer, is famed simply as Padma.
mahabharata:12:343.5	By speech, deed and mind, bull among the twice-born, he pleases beings, standing in the threefold path.
mahabharata:12:343.6	By conciliation, gift, division and punishment, fourfold, he protects people in difficulty and his own with the eye of meditation.
mahabharata:12:343.7	Approaching him by rule, you ought to ask what you wish; he will show you the highest dharma truly.
mahabharata:12:343.8	He is the host of all, the naga, skilled in understanding and the scriptures, joined with all unfailing qualities that please.
mahabharata:12:343.9	By nature always full of water, always devoted to study, joined with austerity and self-control, and with conduct that is not less.

The sight of one cared for in the mind, tender with affection: your word delights me, what you have said.
mahabharata:12:344.5	As if given an eye in space, I see and consider; this instruction I have been given by your wise words I shall carry out fully, as you speak to me.
mahabharata:12:344.6	Stay here tonight with me, good one; in the morning you will go, refreshed and having rested happily. For the blessed sun, of weak rays, faces downward.
[Bhishma said:] Then, honoured as a guest by him, scourge of foes, that guest stayed that night with the twice-born.
While they talked of various things joined with dharma, that whole night passed happily like a day.
Then in the morning that guest, honoured by the brahmana as he could, set out wishing to do his own work.
She, devoted to dharma, duly paid him honour, welcomed him with a greeting and said, "What shall I do?"
[The brahmana said:] "I am rested and honoured by you with your gentle speech; I wish to see, lady, that god, the best of nagas.
This is my highest task and the fruit I wish; for this purpose I have come today to the abode of serpents."
[The naga's wife said:] "Noble one, he has gone to draw the sun's chariot, for his monthly turn; in seven or eight days, Brahmana, he will surely show himself.
This absence of my husband is known to you, noble one; let it be so; what else is to be done, tell me."
All the kinsmen of that naga, brothers, sons and wives, gathered together and went to the brahmana.
They saw him on the bank in a secluded place, firm in his vow, seated, fasting, a brahmana intent on muttering.
All of them, approaching and honouring the brahmana repeatedly, kinsmen of the host, spoke plain words:

This is your sixth day since coming here, ascetic, and you wish for no food, lover of dharma.
mahabharata:12:346.6	You have come to us and we have come to you; hospitality is to be done by us, for we are all householders.
mahabharata:12:346.7	Roots, fruit, leaves, milk or grain, best of the twice-born, you ought to take for food, Brahmana.
mahabharata:12:346.8	With you dwelling in the forest having given up food, all this, children and old, is oppressed by the crisis of dharma.
mahabharata:12:346.9	In this family there has been no slayer of an embryo, no king's bad man, no liar, no eater-first, among gods, guests and kin.
[Bhishma said:] Permitted by that brahmana, the serpents went to their own home, their purpose unfulfilled, bull among men.
The naga questioned his wife, who approached him, endowed with qualities such as washing his feet, a virtuous woman:

Are you, fair one, joined in worshipping gods and guests by the rule told before, as I would be?
mahabharata:12:347.4	Surely your woman's mind has not been softened by his unfulfilled purpose, fair-hipped one, separated by my absence from the bridge of dharma?
[The naga's wife said:] "Service of the teacher for pupils, completion of the Veda for brahmins, obedience to the master for servants, protection of the world for kings,
the protection of all beings is called here kshatriya dharma, and for vaishyas the performance of sacrifice joined with hospitality.
Service of brahmanas, kshatriyas and vaishyas is the shudra's work; the householder's dharma, lord of nagas, is wishing good to all beings.
Constant moderation in food, living the vow in order: dharma is the distinction of the senses by relation to dharma.
'Whose am I, or whence? Who is mine?' Thus with constant thought of purpose one becomes a follower of the stage of liberation.
So I, knowing dharma, with you constant in dharma standing here, how could I leave the good path and go on an uneven way?
O greatly fortunate one, my practice of dharma toward the gods does not fall, and I am constantly unwearied in honouring guests.
Seven or eight days now since a brahmana came here; and he wants to see you, not caring for any other task of mine.
He sits on the bank of the Gomati, eager to see you, repeating Brahman, a brahmana of strict vows.
I, lord of nagas, have been composed by him in conciliation first; I am to be sent to you; the best of serpents has come to him.
Hearing this, greatly wise one, you ought to go there, or you ought to give him sight, Eye-Hearer."

Which man is able, glorious one, wishing to see me, to say beforehand a charming word that commands a meeting?
mahabharata:12:348.3	Among hosts of gods and asuras and divine sages, lady, are the mighty and swift nagas, sons of Surasa, not foremost?
mahabharata:12:348.4	We are to be saluted, givers of boons, and also followers; and especially for men, we are 'treasure-keepers,' so the tradition says.
[The naga's wife said:] "By simplicity I know he is not a god who lives on air; one thing I know of him, he is devoted and very hot-tempered.
He, wishing another purpose, seeking water like a chataka bird, a bird fond of rain, wishes to see you.
No god would wait for you if displeased; born in an equal family, none would attend you.
Therefore, leaving your natural anger, you ought to see him; you ought not to burn yourself by cutting off his hope today.
Kings or princes who have not wiped the tears of those who come in hope are joined to the guilt of killing an embryo.
By giving land one gains a goal equal to a hermitage; having accomplished what is lost, he gains the fruit.
By doing a wished, untroubled act that fulfils desire, no one goes to hell: so say knowers of dharma."
[The naga said:] "My pride is from pride, from the fault of birth my great anger born of resolve has been burnt, virtuous woman, by the fire of your words.
From anger, virtuous woman, I would not see greater darkness, for which serpents especially come to be spoken of.
Fallen under the sway of fault, the mighty Dashagriva, rival of Shakra, was killed by Rama in battle.
Hearing that a calf in the inner apartments had been taken away by Rama, the sons of Kartavirya, troubled with anger at the insult, were slain.
By Rama Jamadagnya, in anger, the mighty Kartavirya, like the thousand-eyed, was slain in battle.
So this enemy of austerities and destroyer of good, anger, has been restrained by me simply on hearing your word.
And I especially praise myself, unfailing one, that you, large-eyed, endowed with all qualities, are my wife.
I go right there where that brahmana stays; since I have said so in every way, he will not go away with his purpose unfulfilled."
Approaching him, the lord of nagas, wise, a king of men, by nature fond of dharma, spoke sweet words:

Ho, ho! I forgive you; I address you; you ought not to make anger. For whose sake have you come here, and with what purpose?
mahabharata:12:349.4	Approaching you face to face, out of affection I ask, twice-born: in a secluded place on the bank of the Gomati, what do you wait for?
[The brahmana said:] "Know me as Dharmaranya, come here to see the naga Padmanabha, best of the twice-born; I have business with him.
I heard of his absence and that he has gone; I wait for my own man like a farmer for rain.
Without causing him trouble, with blessing placed, I live ten thousand days joined with Brahman-yoga, free of ill."
[The naga said:] "Ah, you are of good conduct, a good man fond of good people. You are to be praised, greatly fortunate one, for looking at me with such affection.
I am that naga, brahmana sage, as you find me; command as you wish; what dear thing shall I do for you?"

You are revealed by your own qualities, with rays like the moon's touch, delightful, shining by yourself, with glory in your womb.
mahabharata:12:349.16	The question that has arisen in me, cut it, air-eater; afterward I shall tell my task; you ought to hear me.
[The naga said:] "He in whose thousand rays, as birds in branches, sages dwell, perfected, with the gods,
from whom the great wind issues and spreads in the sky resting in the sun's rays, Brahmana, what is more wonderful than that?
The white, black-banked cloud-bearer in the sky of whom pours water in the rains: what is more wonderful than this?
He who in eight months takes back with his pure ray the water he gave up, at the proper time: what is more wonderful than this?
In his special splendour the self is ever established; from which the seed and this earth with moving and unmoving are held.
Where the god of mighty arms is eternal, supreme, imperishable, without beginning and end, Brahmana: what is more wonderful than this?
Hear this one wonder, as if a wonder of wonders, that I saw in the clear sky, resorting to the sun.
Long ago, at midday, when the sun scorches the worlds, there was seen, in the opposite, one like the sun on every side.
Pervading the light with its beams like a fire fed with oblations, in an indescribable form, like a second sun,
as it approached, Vivasvan gave his hand, and it gave its right hand, wishing to return the honour.
Then, splitting the sky, it entered the sun's disc, and that splendour, become one, in a moment became the sun.
Then a doubt arose in us at the meeting of those two splendours: which of these is the sun, the one standing in the chariot or the one that came?
So we, with doubts arisen, asked the sun: 'Who is this who has gone across the sky like another sun?'"
By Bhargava too, O king of kings, in Janaka's house, this holy story was told to the great-souled Narada.
By Narada too, king of kings, in the house of the lord of the gods, this was told, best of Bharatas, when asked by the one of untroubled deeds.
And long ago by the king of the gods this auspicious story was told to all the praised Vasus, lord of the earth.
And when I had a most terrible battle with Rama, then, O king, this story was told to me by the Vasus.
As you ask in truth, lord of men, I have told you this holy, righteous story, best of upholders of dharma.
This, then, is the supreme dharma that you ask me about, Bharata: steady, free of desire in the acts of dharma and wealth, O king.

And that best of brahmans, having made his resolve, his task pointed out by the lord of serpents, composed in restraint and observance, entered the forest's edge, eating gleaned grain and stones as counted.
Then, O king, that son of Pavaka said to Oghavati: "You must in no way do anything against a guest.
With whatever the guest is pleased, with that you must always serve him; even by giving yourself, you should not hesitate.
This vow of mine ever turns in my heart: for householders, fair-hipped, there is nothing higher than a guest.
If my word is authority for you, fair one, shapely-thighed, keep this word of mine always calmly in your heart.
When I have gone out, dear lady, and while one is near, the guest is not to be slighted by you, if I am authority for you."
Oghavati answered him with joined palms at her head: "There is nothing I will in any way fail to do at your word."
While Sudarshana, wishing to conquer, was at home, Death followed behind him, seeking an opening, always.
When that son of Agni, Sudarshana, had gone for fuel, a glorious brahmana guest said to Oghavati:
I wish for hospitality given by you today, fair one, if the dharma approved in the householder's stage is authority for you.
Thus addressed by that brahmana, the glorious king's daughter received him, lord of men, by the rule told in the Veda.
Having given the twice-born a seat and foot-water, Oghavati said to the brahmana, "What is your need? What shall I give you?"
Then the brahmana said to the king's daughter Sudarshana: "My need is you, fair one; do it without hesitation.
If the dharma approved in the householder's stage is authority for you, queen, you ought to do what I like by giving yourself."
Though pleasing the princess with other desired things, king, the brahmana chose no other boon than her giving herself.
But the king's daughter, remembering her husband's words from the start, said "So be it" to that bull among the twice-born, ashamed.
Then in private the brahmana sage and she sat together, she remembering the husband's words, who desired the householder's stage.
Then, taking the fuel, the son of Agni came, followed by Death in fierce form, as always, like a kinsman.
Then, coming to the hermitage, the son of Agni called Oghavati again and again, "Where have you gone?"
She did not answer her husband then, being touched by the brahmana's hands, the chaste wife devoted to her husband.
Thinking, "I am defiled," ashamed before her husband, the virtuous woman stayed silent and said nothing.
Then Sudarshana again said: "Where is that virtuous one, where has she gone? What is greater than this for me?
Devoted to her husband, true in conduct, ever fond of honesty, why does she not come to meet me today, smiling as before?"
Staying in the hut, the brahmana answered Sudarshana: "Know that a brahmana guest has come, son of Pavaka, and that it is I.
Pleased by your wife with those various honours to a guest, her mind is firm in honesty, best of men.
By this rule this fair-faced one honours me; you ought to say what is fitting here today."
And Death, with a club-hammer in hand, followed him, thinking, "I shall kill him here, who has lost his pledge."
But Sudarshana, with mind, deed, glance and speech, free of envy and anger, said smiling:

May your pleasure be good, best of brahmanas; my joy is the highest; for the householder's foremost dharma is the honouring of a guest who has come.
mahabharata:13:2.69	The householder whose guest goes away honoured: no other dharma is higher than that, say the wise.
mahabharata:13:2.70	My life, my wives and whatever other wealth there is must be given to guests by me: this vow is placed on me.
mahabharata:13:2.71	This word has been spoken by me without doubt; by this truth, Brahmana, I touch my own self.
mahabharata:13:2.72	Earth, wind, space, water and fire as the fifth, intellect, self, mind, time and the directions: ten qualities.
mahabharata:13:2.73	These always see, dwelling in the bodies of the embodied, the good and the evil deeds, best of upholders of dharma.
mahabharata:13:2.74	As this speech has not been untrue as spoken by me today, by that truth let the gods protect me or burn me.
Then a sound arose in all directions, Bharata, repeatedly: "True! This is not false!" on every side.
Then that brahmana came out of the hut, rising like the wind and pervading sky and earth with his body.
With the phonetic voice, making the three worlds resound, the brahmana, having first addressed the knower of dharma by name, said:

I am Dharma; good fortune to you, sinless one; I came to test you, and knowing your truth my joy in you is highest.
mahabharata:13:2.79	Death, who follows you, seeking an opening always, has been conquered by you and subdued by your steadiness.
mahabharata:13:2.80	There is no power in the three worlds, best of men, in anyone even to look at this virtuous wife devoted to her husband.
mahabharata:13:2.81	She is guarded by your qualities and by the qualities of a devoted wife; unassailable, what she says will be so, not otherwise.
mahabharata:13:2.82	Joined by her own austerity, a speaker of Brahman, for the purification of the world she will be the best of rivers.
mahabharata:13:2.83	She, greatly fortunate, named Oghavati, will follow you with half her body; yoga is within her control.
mahabharata:13:2.84	With her you will go to the worlds won by austerity, eternal, from which there is no return.
mahabharata:13:2.85	And with this body you will reach the worlds; death is conquered by you and your lordship is supreme.
mahabharata:13:2.86	You have passed beyond the five elements and from your own power the mind-born; by this householder's dharma desire and anger are conquered by you.
mahabharata:13:2.87	Affection, passion, sloth, delusion and malice entire, O king, have been conquered by your service to the king's daughter.
[Bhishma said:] Then the blessed Vyavasaya, taking an excellent chariot yoked with a thousand white horses, went to him.
Death, the self, the worlds, the five elements, intellect, time, mind, space, and desire and anger were conquered.
Therefore for one standing in the householder's stage there is no other god than the guest, tiger among men; reflect on this in mind.
The guest honoured by whom meditates in mind on the good: the wise say that is not equalled even by a hundred sacrifices.
One who, meeting a guest who is a worthy vessel and rich in conduct, does not honour him, having given, destroys his merit, being unhonoured.
This excellent story has been told to you, son, of how Death was conquered long ago by a householder.
This excellent story, bringing wealth, fame and long life, is to be honoured by those who wish to prosper, and removes all misdeeds.
The learned man who tells this day after day, Bharata, the deeds of Sudarshana, would gain holy worlds.
[Yudhishthira said:] I wish to hear in truth how Vishvamitra, righteous-souled bull among men, attained brahminhood; tell me, grandfather.
For that one of boundless might, by austerity, instantly slew the hundred sons of the great-souled Vasishtha, great-grandfather.
And many Yatudhanas, rakshasas of sharp splendour, were created by him with a body possessed by anger, like Time the Ender.
And the lineage of the great Kushika, crowded with hundreds of Brahmarishis, was established in this world of men, learned and praised by brahmins.
Shunahshepa, Richika's son, of great austerity, was released from the great sacrifice when he had become a victim.
In the sacrifice of Harishchandra, having pleased the gods with his own splendour, he became the son of the wise Vishvamitra.
He did not salute the eldest, Devarata, king; and five hundred sons were cursed and became dog-cookers.
Trishanku, abandoned by kin, an Ikshvaku, was lovingly taken to heaven head downward, relying on the southern quarter.
You ought to tell all this to me in truth, king, and tell me truly of Matanga just as it is.
Rightly Matanga did not gain brahminhood, best of Bharatas; born in a Chandala womb, how could he attain brahminhood?
[Bhishma said:] In Bharata's line there was a king named Ajamidha, best of Bharatas, a sacrificer, best of upholders of dharma.
His son was the king Jahnu, whose daughter Ganga became, the great soul's.
His son of equal qualities was Sindhudvipa of great fame; from Sindhudvipa the royal sage Balakashva of great strength.
His son was Vallabha, as if another Dharma himself; his son was Kushika, radiant like the thousand-eyed.
Kushika's son was the glorious king named Gadhi; childless, the mighty-armed one dwelt in the forest.
A daughter was born to him as he lived in the forest, named Satyavati, of incomparable beauty on earth.
The glorious Bhargava, Chyavana's son, the lord, famed as Richika, firm in great austerity, asked for her.
Gadhi, slayer of foes, did not give her to that great-souled Richika, thinking him poor.
Near Kanyakubja, on the excellent bank of the Ganga, is a place that men even today call Ashvatirtha.
There Richika, best of mutterers, pleased, gave Gadhi a thousand fine horses for the bride-price.
Then King Gadhi, astonished and from fear of a curse, adorned the maiden and gave her to Bhrigu's son.
That best of Brahmarishis took her hand by rule, and she, reaching her husband, gained great joy.
The brahmana sage was pleased with her conduct, Bharata, and he offered the fair-complexioned one a boon.
She told all that to her mother, the king's best; then her mother said to the daughter, who had her face lowered somewhat:
Daughter, your husband ought to show favour to me also; that great ascetic is able to grant offspring.
Then she quickly went and told him all this, her mother's wish, king, and Richika said to her:

You and she will bear virtuous offspring; let there be no other desire for your mother, fair one.
mahabharata:13:4.26	A son proud of your qualities will be born to you, auspicious one, glorious, a maker of our line; and your brother will be a maker of line.
mahabharata:13:4.27	When she is bathed after her season, you embrace the ashvattha tree, and she the udumbara tree, fair one; then you will gain what you wish.
mahabharata:13:4.28	And this pair of oblations purified with mantras, bright-smiled one: you and she should eat them; then you will get sons.
Then Satyavati, glad, said to her mother what Richika had said, and told her of the two oblations.
Then her mother said to her daughter Satyavati: "Daughter, who bows her head to you, do my word.
This oblation given you by your husband, prefaced with mantras: give it to me, and take mine yourself.
And let us two exchange the trees also, bright-smiled one, if my word is authority, blameless one, as mother's.
Surely the blessed one has done so here; then my mind, slender-waisted, is on your oblation and the tree; think how your brother should be distinguished."
And so they did, mother and Satyavati; then both of them reached the embryo, Yudhishthira.
Seeing his wife come to the embryo, that great sage, best of Bhrigus, unhappy, said to Satyavati:

The oblation you ate was exchanged; it will be seen; the trees were also exchanged, plainly, by you, fair one.
mahabharata:13:4.37	By me, whatever Brahman there is in the world was placed in your oblation, and all kshatriya power was placed in hers.
mahabharata:13:4.38	You would have borne a brahmana of qualities famed in the three worlds; and she a distinguished kshatriya; this was made by me.
mahabharata:13:4.39	But because the exchange was made by you and your mother, therefore your mother will bear the best of brahmanas.
mahabharata:13:4.40	And you, fair one, will bear a kshatriya of fierce deeds; that was not well done by you out of love for your mother, lady.
Hearing it, Satyavati, tormented with grief, O king, fell to the ground like a lovely creeper cut.
Regaining consciousness and bowing her head, Gadhi's daughter said to her husband, the best of brahmanas:

As I your wife entreat you, best of knowers of Brahman, show favour, brahmana sage: let me not have a kshatriya son.
mahabharata:13:4.44	Let my grandson be of fierce deeds if you wish, but let my son not be so, Brahmana; let this boon be given me.
So be it, said the great ascetic to his wife; then she bore the auspicious son Jamadagni.
And the glorious wife of Gadhi's son bore Vishvamitra, by the sage's power, O king, a Brahmarishi, a speaker of Brahman.
Then Vishvamitra of great austerity, though a kshatriya, attained brahminhood, and thus became the founder of a Brahman line.
[Brihaspati said:] "I do not wish to sacrifice for you, lord of the earth; I am chosen by the king of the gods, and that was promised to him."
Having regained his breath, King Dhritarashtra embraced the Pandava with his arms and smelled his head.
Thinking himself guilty, he seized his feet with his head, in distress; and the great soul comforted him then, going upward, filling heaven and earth with his glory.
Thus addressed, the royal sage, your ancestor, went with Dharma and with all those in the abodes of the gods.
